sections.text:
Mangroves on the Front Line

A. Along sheltered tropical and subtropical coastlines, where rivers meet the sea, a peculiar kind of forest stands with its feet in salt water. Mangroves are not a single species but a collection of trees and shrubs, drawn from several unrelated plant families, that have independently evolved ways of surviving conditions that would kill most land plants. With each high tide, seawater floods their roots; as the tide retreats, it exposes soft, airless mud. Some species cope by filtering salt out at the roots, while others take it in and excrete it through glands on their leaves. Many send up pencil-like roots from the mud, which act as snorkels, allowing the buried root system to breathe. Others are propped up on arching stilt roots that make the forest look as though it is walking into the water.

B. It is this tangle of roots and trunks that makes mangroves so valuable to the people who live behind them. When waves enter a mangrove belt, they lose energy through friction as water is forced around countless obstacles. In a study on a low-lying delta coast, coastal engineer Nirmala Seneviratne placed pressure sensors at intervals through a forest 300 metres wide and recorded conditions over two monsoon seasons. She found that the height of ordinary waves fell by around 60 per cent between the seaward edge and the landward edge. Seneviratne is careful not to overstate the result. Exceptionally powerful storm surges, she notes, can push water through even a healthy forest, and a narrow fringe of trees offers far less protection than a broad one. Nevertheless, in her view, a wide belt can do much of the work of a concrete sea wall at a fraction of the cost, and unlike a wall it repairs itself.

C. Mangroves also shape the land itself. Their roots slow the movement of water so that fine particles carried by rivers and tides settle out instead of being washed away. Over time this trapped sediment, together with decaying roots, raises the forest floor. Where enough sediment is available, the ground can build up quickly enough to keep pace with the rising sea, something no artificial barrier can do. The same waterlogged soils lock away remarkable quantities of carbon, because dead plant material decomposes very slowly in the absence of oxygen. Researchers have found that, area for area, mangrove forests can store several times as much carbon as many forests on dry land, mostly in their soils. The shallow channels between the roots, meanwhile, shelter young fish, shrimp and crabs, many of which are later caught by fishers once they move into open water.

D. Despite these benefits, mangroves have been cleared on a vast scale. A substantial share of the world's mangrove area has disappeared since the middle of the twentieth century. In parts of Southeast Asia and Latin America, a major cause was the spread of shrimp farming: forests were cut down and replaced by rectangular ponds enclosed by earth walls. Such ponds were often productive for only a few years before disease and accumulated waste forced owners to abandon them and clear new ground. Elsewhere, mangroves gave way to rice paddies, oil palm plantations, ports and tourist resorts, or were thinned for timber and charcoal. Because the forests occupied land that seemed to have no owner and no obvious use, their destruction attracted little attention until coastal communities began to notice increased flooding and smaller catches. The rate of loss has slowed considerably in recent years, partly because the value of the forests is now more widely understood.

E. Replanting has become popular with governments, charities and companies, but early efforts produced disappointing results. Ecologist Esteban Ruvalcaba visited 46 restoration sites along one stretch of coast and counted how many trees were still alive five years after planting. Where volunteers had pushed seedlings into open mudflats below the natural forest edge, survival was often under 10 per cent: the young trees spent too long underwater each day and were swept away or drowned. Projects that planted a single fast-growing species in neat rows did somewhat better but created plantations that supported few animals. The most successful sites, Ruvalcaba found, were abandoned shrimp ponds where the earth walls had simply been broken open. Once tidal water could flow in and out again, seeds arrived naturally from nearby forests, and after five years these sites held a richer mix of species than any of the planted ones. His conclusion is that restoring the right water conditions often matters more than planting itself.

F. Even a well-designed project can fail if the people living nearby see no reason to protect it. Social scientist Adaeze Nwosu compared villages where restoration had been organised by outside agencies with villages where residents had helped to choose the sites and set the rules. In the second group, young forests were far less likely to be cut down again within a decade. Nwosu points in particular to agreements that gave local families the right to collect crabs from the restored areas, which turned the forest into a source of income worth defending. Her work suggests that mangroves will only hold the line against the sea if they are also valued by those who live on the shore.

sections.text:
From Chains to Satellites

A. Until well into the twentieth century, a detailed map of a country began with people walking across it. Surveyors carried measuring chains, heavy brass instruments and notebooks, and they depended on triangulation, a technique borrowed from geometry. A team would first measure a single straight line on flat ground, called a baseline, with great care, sometimes over several weeks. From each end of this line they sighted a distant landmark, such as a church tower or a hilltop, and recorded the angles. Because one side and two angles are enough to fix the rest of a triangle, the surveyors could calculate distances they had never walked, then use each new side as the starting point for another triangle. In this way a chain of triangles gradually spread across the landscape.

B. The method was accurate but painfully slow. Large national surveys in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries took decades to complete, and survey parties endured heat, disease and harsh weather while hauling equipment up hills. Yet according to Anneke Vos, a historian of cartography, the physical hardship is only part of the story. After studying the field notebooks of several surveys, she argues that the finished maps concealed countless small decisions: which villages to record, whose spelling of a place name to adopt, and which paths were important enough to draw. Some of these choices, she adds, were made by surveyors who did not speak the local language. 'A map looks like a neutral picture,' she writes, 'but every line on it was chosen by someone standing in a particular place.'

C. The first great acceleration came from the air. After the First World War, cameras mounted in aircraft were used to photograph large areas in overlapping strips. Specialists then examined pairs of these images through stereoscopes, instruments that made the ground appear three-dimensional and allowed the height of hills and valleys to be measured. This technique, known as photogrammetry, did not abolish fieldwork – someone still had to visit the ground to name features and check fixed points – but it reduced the walking dramatically. Aerial photographs also captured details, such as the precise outline of a coastline or the edge of a forest, that a surveyor on foot could easily misjudge. A district that might once have occupied a survey party for several seasons could now be photographed in a few days.

D. Satellites changed the scale once again. From 1972, satellites designed to study the Earth's surface began sending back regular images of almost every part of the planet, allowing map-makers to track changes such as spreading cities, retreating glaciers and new roads. Later, satellite navigation systems let anyone with a receiver work out their position by timing signals from several satellites at once. For years civilian users received a deliberately degraded signal, but in 2000 this restriction was switched off, and ordinary receivers became accurate to within a few metres. Efosa Delgado, a geographer who compared old triangulation points with their modern satellite positions, found that many nineteenth-century measurements were out by less than a metre. He attributes this not to the quality of the surveyors' instruments but to their habit of repeating every angle many times and averaging the results.

E. Perhaps the deepest change, however, lies not in how information is collected but in how it is stored. A printed map is a finished object; once the ink is dry, correcting it means printing a new edition. Digital mapping systems instead keep information in separate layers – roads, rivers, buildings, land use – that can be combined, updated or hidden at will. This has made maps far cheaper to revise, but it has also shifted the main problem from gathering information to managing it. Shirin Farouk, who studies volunteer mapping projects, notes that thousands of unpaid contributors now add streets and buildings to online maps. In her research on one coastal region, volunteers recorded footpaths and small shops that appeared on no government map. She also found, however, that coverage was uneven: wealthy urban districts were mapped in fine detail, while poorer rural areas received far less attention.

F. The way people use maps has changed as well. Pavel Kimura, who researches human navigation, asked two groups of walkers to cross an unfamiliar town, one following turn-by-turn directions on a phone and the other using a paper map. Those guided by the phone arrived slightly sooner and made fewer wrong turns, but when asked afterwards to sketch their route, they produced far less accurate drawings. Kimura suggests that when a device takes over the work of orientation, people pay less attention to landmarks, although he cautions that his study involved only short journeys.

G. For all these changes, some things remain remarkably constant. Satellite positions are still checked against fixed markers on the ground, and map-makers continue to face the questions that troubled their predecessors: what to include, what to leave out and what to call it. The tools have moved from the hillside into orbit, but the judgement behind every map is still a human one.

questions.prompt: Looking at two overlapping aerial photographs together made it possible to measure differences in the height of the land.
questions.evidence: allowed the height of hills and valleys to be measured

explanation.en: Paragraph C explains that pairs of overlapping images viewed through stereoscopes looked three-dimensional and allowed the height of hills and valleys to be measured.
explanation.ru: В абзаце C объясняется, что пары перекрывающихся снимков при просмотре через стереоскоп выглядели объёмными и позволяли измерять высоту холмов и долин.
explanation.uk: В абзаці C пояснюється, що пари знімків, які перекривалися, під час перегляду через стереоскоп виглядали об'ємними й дозволяли вимірювати висоту пагорбів і долин.

questions.prompt: Once aerial photography was introduced, mapping no longer required anyone to visit the area in person.
questions.evidence: did not abolish fieldwork

explanation.en: Paragraph C says photogrammetry did not abolish fieldwork, because someone still had to visit the ground to name features and check points. Fieldwork was reduced, not removed.
explanation.ru: В абзаце C сказано, что фотограмметрия не отменила полевые работы: кому-то всё равно нужно было выезжать на местность, чтобы давать названия объектам и проверять точки. Полевых работ стало меньше, но они не исчезли.
explanation.uk: В абзаці C сказано, що фотограмметрія не скасувала польових робіт: комусь однаково треба було виїжджати на місцевість, щоб давати назви об'єктам і перевіряти точки. Польових робіт поменшало, але вони не зникли.

questions.prompt: Satellite images have shown that glaciers are shrinking faster than scientists had predicted.

explanation.en: Paragraph D only says satellites let map-makers track changes such as retreating glaciers. It says nothing about how fast they are shrinking or about scientists' predictions.
explanation.ru: В абзаце D говорится лишь о том, что спутники позволяют картографам отслеживать изменения, например отступание ледников. О том, как быстро ледники уменьшаются, и о прогнозах учёных там ничего не сказано.
explanation.uk: В абзаці D лише сказано, що супутники дозволяють картографам відстежувати зміни, наприклад відступ льодовиків. Про те, як швидко льодовики зменшуються, і про прогнози науковців там нічого не сказано.

questions.prompt: After a restriction was removed in 2000, ordinary satellite receivers could find positions to within a few metres.
questions.evidence: in 2000 this restriction was switched off, and ordinary receivers became accurate to within a few metres

explanation.en: Paragraph D says the deliberate weakening of civilian signals was switched off in 2000, and receivers then became accurate to within a few metres.
explanation.ru: В абзаце D сказано, что намеренное ухудшение гражданского сигнала отключили в 2000 году, и после этого приёмники стали определять положение с точностью до нескольких метров.
explanation.uk: В абзаці D сказано, що навмисне погіршення цивільного сигналу вимкнули у 2000 році, і після цього приймачі стали визначати місцезнаходження з точністю до кількох метрів.

questions.prompt: Depending on a device for directions may make people less aware of their surroundings.
questions.evidence: when a device takes over the work of orientation, people pay less attention to landmarks

explanation.en: In paragraph F, Pavel Kimura suggests that people who follow phone directions notice landmarks less.
explanation.ru: В абзаце F Pavel Kimura предполагает, что люди, которые следуют подсказкам навигатора в телефоне, реже замечают ориентиры.
explanation.uk: В абзаці F Pavel Kimura припускає, що люди, які йдуть за підказками навігатора в телефоні, менше помічають орієнтири.

questions.prompt: Maps that seem objective actually reflect many choices made by individuals.
questions.evidence: the finished maps concealed countless small decisions

explanation.en: In paragraph B, Anneke Vos argues that maps look neutral but hide many decisions, such as which names and paths to include.
explanation.ru: В абзаце B Anneke Vos утверждает, что карты кажутся нейтральными, но за ними скрывается множество решений — например, какие названия и тропы на них показывать.
explanation.uk: В абзаці B Anneke Vos стверджує, що мапи здаються нейтральними, але за ними приховано багато рішень — наприклад, які назви та стежки на них показувати.

groups.instruction: Look at the following statements and the list of people below. Match each statement with the correct person, A–D. You may use any letter more than once.

questions.prompt: Traditional surveys started with a carefully measured straight line, known as a ______, from whose ends angles to distant landmarks were taken.
questions.evidence: a single straight line on flat ground, called a baseline

explanation.en: Paragraph A says the team first measured a straight line called a baseline and then sighted landmarks from each end.
explanation.ru: В абзаце A сказано, что сначала команда измеряла прямую линию, которая называется "baseline" (базис), а затем с каждого её конца засекала ориентиры.
explanation.uk: В абзаці A сказано, що спершу команда вимірювала пряму лінію, яка називається "baseline" (базис), а потім з кожного її кінця візувала орієнтири.

questions.prompt: After the First World War, specialists viewed pairs of aerial photographs through ______, which gave the landscape a three-dimensional appearance.
questions.evidence: examined pairs of these images through stereoscopes

explanation.en: Paragraph C says specialists examined overlapping images through stereoscopes, which made the ground look three-dimensional.
explanation.ru: В абзаце C сказано, что специалисты рассматривали перекрывающиеся снимки через стереоскопы ("stereoscopes"), и благодаря этому местность выглядела объёмной.
explanation.uk: В абзаці C сказано, що фахівці розглядали знімки, які перекривалися, через стереоскопи ("stereoscopes"), і завдяки цьому місцевість виглядала об'ємною.

questions.prompt: Today, digital systems store different kinds of information, such as roads and rivers, in separate ______ that can be combined or hidden.
questions.evidence: keep information in separate layers

explanation.en: Paragraph E says digital mapping systems keep information in separate layers that can be combined, updated or hidden.
explanation.ru: В абзаце E сказано, что цифровые картографические системы хранят информацию в отдельных слоях ("layers"), которые можно объединять, обновлять или скрывать.
explanation.uk: В абзаці E сказано, що цифрові картографічні системи зберігають інформацію в окремих шарах ("layers"), які можна поєднувати, оновлювати або приховувати.

groups.instruction: Complete the summary below. Choose NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS from the passage for each answer.

sections.text:
Fewer Days, Better Work?

A. For most of the last century, the five-day week has seemed as fixed as the calendar itself. Yet it is a social invention, not a law of nature: the two-day weekend became common only after long campaigns by workers and a recognition by some employers that rested staff were more productive. Today a growing number of organisations are asking whether the next step is a third day off. My own view is that the idea deserves to be taken seriously, but not in the form in which it is often sold. A four-day week is worth having only if it changes how work is done, not merely when it is done.

B. The case in favour begins with a simple observation: hours at a desk are not the same as useful output. Sunniva Halvorsen, an organisational psychologist, tracked forty office teams over a year and found that a large share of the working day was consumed by meetings that participants themselves rated as unnecessary. When her teams moved to four days while keeping full pay, most cut their meetings by around a third and reported that they protected long blocks of uninterrupted time for demanding tasks. Output, measured by projects completed on schedule, remained broadly stable. Halvorsen is careful to note that her teams volunteered for the trial, so they may have been unusually motivated, but the pattern is hard to dismiss.

C. Health is the second argument. Mei-Ling Arkwright, who studies occupational wellbeing, compared sickness absence in firms before and after a reduction in days. Absence fell in almost every case, and staff described sleeping better and feeling less exhausted on Monday mornings. Arkwright points out, however, that the benefits were concentrated among employees who genuinely stopped working on their extra day. Those who continued to answer emails from home reported little improvement. In other words, a day off that is not really off brings few gains. Her conclusion is that a reduced week works best when managers make it clear that nobody is expected to be reachable on the free day.

D. It is here that the most common version of the policy goes wrong. Many employers, attracted by the headline but nervous about lost hours, introduce a "compressed" week, in which the same forty hours are squeezed into four ten-hour days. Adebayo Whitcombe, a labour economist, argues that this simply moves fatigue around. In his study of warehouse and call-centre staff on compressed schedules, error rates rose sharply in the final two hours of each long shift, wiping out much of the benefit of the extra rest day. I find his evidence persuasive. A shorter week that is achieved by making each day longer misunderstands why fewer hours can help in the first place.

E. Critics raise a different objection: that the four-day week suits only certain kinds of job. A software developer can perhaps finish the same work in less time; a nurse cannot care for patients who are not there. Jonas Esterhuizen, a consultant who works with service organisations, has observed that hospitals, schools and shops must keep their doors open regardless of staff schedules, so a reduced week for each worker means hiring more people or arranging complicated rotas. He describes the cost of this extra staffing as the "hidden bill" that enthusiastic reports tend to ignore. This is a fair point, and supporters who claim the policy will pay for itself everywhere are, in my view, overstating their case.

F. A further concern is fairness within the workforce. Paulina Ndiaye, a sociologist, interviewed employees at firms that had adopted four-day schedules for some departments but not others. She found that resentment grew quickly where front-line staff kept five days while head-office colleagues enjoyed three-day weekends. Several interviewees said the arrangement made them feel like second-class employees, even when their pay was unchanged. Ndiaye suggests that employers should offer comparable benefits, such as shorter shifts or additional annual leave, to groups whose roles cannot be reorganised. Whether such alternatives are valued as highly as a full extra day off remains, she admits, an open question.

G. None of these difficulties seems to me a reason to abandon the idea. They are reasons to introduce it carefully. The organisations that have succeeded tend to share three features: they began with a limited trial, they measured results rather than hours, and they removed tasks instead of compressing them. Those that failed usually tried to change everything at once, or quietly raised targets so that staff ended up working on their supposed day off. Governments could help by funding trials in sectors where the practical obstacles are greatest, since these are precisely the settings about which we know least.

H. The five-day week was once a radical proposal too. Its defenders did not argue that every job could be organised identically; they argued that people work better when they have time to recover. That principle still holds, perhaps more than ever in an age of constant digital connection. The question is not whether we can afford a four-day week, but whether we are willing to do the harder work of deciding which of our current tasks actually matter.
sections.title: Fewer Days, Better Work?

questions.prompt: The five-day working week developed naturally rather than as a result of human decisions.
questions.evidence: it is a social invention, not a law of nature

explanation.en: In paragraph A the writer says the five-day week is a social invention and not a law of nature, which is the opposite of the statement.
explanation.ru: В абзаце A автор говорит, что пятидневная рабочая неделя — это изобретение общества, а не закон природы. Это прямо противоречит утверждению.
explanation.uk: В абзаці A автор зазначає, що п'ятиденний робочий тиждень — це суспільний винахід, а не закон природи. Це прямо суперечить твердженню.

questions.prompt: Halvorsen's results can be ignored because the teams in her study chose to take part.
questions.evidence: so they may have been unusually motivated, but the pattern is hard to dismiss

explanation.en: In paragraph B the writer accepts that the volunteers may have been very motivated, but says the pattern is hard to dismiss, so the writer does not think the results should be ignored.
explanation.ru: В абзаце B автор признаёт, что добровольцы, возможно, были очень мотивированы, но говорит, что от этой закономерности трудно отмахнуться. Значит, автор не считает, что результаты можно игнорировать.
explanation.uk: В абзаці B автор визнає, що добровольці, можливо, були дуже вмотивовані, але каже, що цю закономірність важко відкинути. Отже, автор не вважає, що результати можна ігнорувати.

questions.prompt: Fitting a full week's hours into four longer days is a mistaken way to shorten the week.
questions.evidence: A shorter week that is achieved by making each day longer misunderstands why fewer hours can help in the first place.

explanation.en: In paragraph D the writer agrees with Whitcombe and says that making each day longer misunderstands why fewer hours help, so the writer sees this approach as a mistake.
explanation.ru: В абзаце D автор соглашается с Whitcombe и говорит, что удлинять каждый рабочий день — значит не понимать, почему меньшее количество часов приносит пользу. Значит, автор считает такой подход ошибкой.
explanation.uk: В абзаці D автор погоджується з Whitcombe і каже, що подовжувати кожен робочий день — означає не розуміти, чому менша кількість годин дає користь. Отже, автор вважає такий підхід помилкою.

questions.prompt: Hospital workers generally experience more stress than people who work in offices.

explanation.en: Paragraph E mentions nurses and hospitals only to show that some services must stay open. The writer does not compare stress levels between hospital staff and office workers.
explanation.ru: В абзаце E медсёстры и больницы упоминаются лишь для того, чтобы показать, что некоторые службы должны продолжать работать. Автор не сравнивает уровень стресса у персонала больниц и офисных работников.
explanation.uk: В абзаці E медсестри й лікарні згадуються лише для того, щоб показати, що деякі служби мають працювати й далі. Автор не порівнює рівень стресу в персоналу лікарень і офісних працівників.

questions.prompt: Some people who support the four-day week exaggerate how affordable it will be.
questions.evidence: supporters who claim the policy will pay for itself everywhere are, in my view, overstating their case

explanation.en: In paragraph E the writer says that supporters who claim the policy will pay for itself everywhere are overstating their case, which means exaggerating its affordability.
explanation.ru: В абзаце E автор говорит, что сторонники, которые утверждают, будто такая политика везде окупится, перегибают палку. То есть они преувеличивают, насколько эта мера доступна по затратам.
explanation.uk: В абзаці E автор каже, що прихильники, які стверджують, ніби ця політика скрізь окупиться, перебільшують. Тобто вони перебільшують, наскільки цей захід доступний за витратами.

groups.instruction: Do the following statements agree with the views of the writer in the passage? Write YES if the statement agrees with the views of the writer, NO if the statement contradicts the views of the writer, or NOT GIVEN if it is impossible to say what the writer thinks about this.

options.text: lengthening each of the remaining working days.
recruiting extra workers or devising more complex rotas.
kept replying to work messages on their extra day.
introduce the change across the whole organisation at once.
a rise in mistakes during the last part of each shift.
reducing the time they spent in meetings.
only some departments were moved to a four-day schedule.
took no sick leave at all during the trial.
judge performance by what was achieved rather than by hours.
a sharp fall in output on the extra rest day.

questions.prompt: Halvorsen's teams responded to working four days by
questions.evidence: most cut their meetings by around a third

explanation.en: Paragraph B says most of Halvorsen's teams cut their meetings by about a third. The passage does not say they made their days longer.
explanation.ru: В абзаце B сказано, что большинство команд Halvorsen сократили количество совещаний примерно на треть. О том, что они удлинили рабочий день, в тексте не говорится.
explanation.uk: В абзаці B сказано, що більшість команд Halvorsen скоротили кількість нарад приблизно на третину. Про те, що вони подовжили робочий день, у тексті не йдеться.

questions.prompt: Arkwright found that the health benefits were small for employees who
questions.evidence: Those who continued to answer emails from home reported little improvement.

explanation.en: Paragraph C says staff who continued to answer emails from home on their day off saw little improvement. Nothing is said about staff taking no sick leave at all.
explanation.ru: В абзаце C говорится, что у сотрудников, которые в свой выходной продолжали отвечать на письма из дома, улучшения были незначительными. О сотрудниках, которые вообще не брали больничный, ничего не сказано.
explanation.uk: В абзаці C ідеться про те, що в працівників, які у свій вихідний і далі відповідали на листи з дому, покращення були незначними. Про працівників, які взагалі не брали лікарняного, нічого не сказано.

questions.prompt: Whitcombe's research showed that long shifts led to
questions.evidence: error rates rose sharply in the final two hours of each long shift

explanation.en: Paragraph D reports that errors rose sharply in the last two hours of each long shift. The passage does not mention output falling on the rest day.
explanation.ru: В абзаце D сообщается, что в последние два часа каждой длинной смены количество ошибок резко возрастало. О снижении производительности в день отдыха в тексте не упоминается.
explanation.uk: В абзаці D повідомляється, що в останні дві години кожної довгої зміни кількість помилок різко зростала. Про зниження продуктивності в день відпочинку в тексті не згадується.

questions.prompt: Esterhuizen points out that in services which must stay open, a shorter week for each worker means
questions.evidence: a reduced week for each worker means hiring more people or arranging complicated rotas

explanation.en: Paragraph E says hospitals, schools and shops would need to hire more people or arrange complicated rotas, which matches recruiting extra workers or devising complex rotas.
explanation.ru: В абзаце E сказано, что больницам, школам и магазинам пришлось бы нанимать больше людей или составлять сложные графики смен. Это соответствует найму дополнительных работников или разработке сложных графиков.
explanation.uk: В абзаці E сказано, що лікарням, школам і магазинам довелося б наймати більше людей або складати складні графіки змін. Це відповідає найму додаткових працівників чи розробленню складних графіків.

questions.prompt: Ndiaye found that staff became resentful in workplaces where
questions.evidence: resentment grew quickly where front-line staff kept five days while head-office colleagues enjoyed three-day weekends

explanation.en: Paragraph F says resentment grew when some staff kept five days while others had three-day weekends, meaning only some departments got the shorter week.
explanation.ru: В абзаце F сказано, что недовольство росло, когда одни сотрудники по-прежнему работали пять дней, а у других были трёхдневные выходные. Значит, сокращённую неделю получили лишь некоторые отделы.
explanation.uk: В абзаці F сказано, що невдоволення зростало, коли одні працівники й далі працювали п'ять днів, а інші мали триденні вихідні. Отже, скорочений тиждень отримали лише деякі відділи.

groups.instruction: Complete each sentence with the correct ending, A–J, from the box below. There are more endings than sentences, so you will not use them all.

questions.prompt: In Halvorsen's study, output was judged by the number of projects that were finished ______.
questions.evidence: Output, measured by projects completed on schedule, remained broadly stable.

explanation.en: Paragraph B says output was measured by projects completed on schedule; 'finished' in the sentence restates 'completed'.
explanation.ru: В абзаце B сказано, что результаты работы измерялись количеством проектов ("projects"), завершённых в срок; слово "finished" в предложении — это перефразировка слова "completed".
explanation.uk: В абзаці B сказано, що результати роботи вимірювали кількістю проєктів ("projects"), завершених вчасно; слово "finished" у реченні — це перефразування слова "completed".

questions.prompt: Arkwright looked at levels of ______ in companies before and after they cut the number of working days.
questions.evidence: compared sickness absence in firms before and after a reduction in days

explanation.en: Paragraph C says Arkwright compared sickness absence in firms before and after the number of days was reduced.
explanation.ru: В абзаце C сказано, что Arkwright сравнила отсутствие на работе по болезни ("sickness absence") в компаниях до и после того, как количество рабочих дней сократили.
explanation.uk: В абзаці C сказано, що Arkwright порівняла відсутність на роботі через хворобу ("sickness absence") у компаніях до та після того, як кількість робочих днів скоротили.

questions.prompt: Whitcombe believes that a compressed week only shifts ______ from one part of the week to another.
questions.evidence: argues that this simply moves fatigue around

explanation.en: Paragraph D says Whitcombe argues that the compressed week simply moves fatigue around instead of reducing it.
explanation.ru: В абзаце D сказано, что Whitcombe утверждает: сжатая рабочая неделя просто перераспределяет усталость ("fatigue"), а не уменьшает её.
explanation.uk: В абзаці D сказано, що Whitcombe стверджує: стиснутий робочий тиждень просто перерозподіляє втому ("fatigue"), а не зменшує її.

questions.prompt: Esterhuizen uses the term ______ for the cost of extra staff, which positive reports often overlook.
questions.evidence: He describes the cost of this extra staffing as the "hidden bill"

explanation.en: Paragraph E says Esterhuizen calls the cost of extra staffing the 'hidden bill' that enthusiastic reports tend to ignore.
explanation.ru: В абзаце E сказано, что Esterhuizen называет расходы на дополнительный персонал "hidden bill" — скрытым счётом, который восторженные отчёты обычно не учитывают.
explanation.uk: В абзаці E сказано, що Esterhuizen називає витрати на додатковий персонал "hidden bill" — прихованим рахунком, який захоплені звіти зазвичай не враховують.
